usage: 내다 is the standard verb for paying taxes, bills, fees
붙다 (to stick) is how Koreans say tax/fees are tacked onto a price
신고 = official declaration; 종합소득세 신고 is the yearly income-tax filing
환급 is the refund you get back, e.g. 연말정산 환급 at year-end
examples: 월급에서 세금이 자동으로 빠져요.
Tax comes out of my paycheck automatically.
빠지다 here = to be deducted; common for 4대보험·세금
이 가격에 세금이 포함돼 있나요?
Is tax included in this price?
Useful when a quote looks suspiciously low; 부가세 별도 means VAT not included
프리랜서는 세금을 직접 신고해야 돼요.
Freelancers have to file taxes themselves.
Relevant for foreigners doing 3.3% 사업소득 work
nuance: 세금 is the general word covering income tax, VAT, property tax and more. In daily life you mostly hear it about your paycheck (소득세 빠진다) or when checking if 부가세 is included in a price. For the once-a-year reckoning, people say 연말정산 (year-end settlement) rather than 세금 itself.
mistakes: Saying 세금을 사다 — you 내다 (pay) tax, never 사다.
Confusing 세금 (tax) with 요금 (a usage fee/fare); your phone bill is 요금, not 세금.

usage: The mandatory state pension; foreigners on certain visas pay in too
받다 for the money you collect after retirement
가입하다 is the verb for joining/signing up for any scheme
개인 = personal; a voluntary retirement savings product from a bank or insurer
examples: 국민연금은 월급에서 매달 빠져나가요.
National pension is taken out of my salary every month.
빠져나가다 = to be withdrawn/deducted automatically
저는 노후를 위해 개인연금도 들었어요.
I also signed up for a private pension for my old age.
들다 (to sign up) is colloquial for joining insurance/pension; 노후 = later life
연금을 언제부터 받을 수 있어요?
From when can I start receiving the pension?
Practical question about the payout age (currently rising past 60)
nuance: 연금 usually means 국민연금, the compulsory national pension deducted from your pay. Some foreigners can claim a lump-sum refund (반환일시금) when they leave Korea, depending on their country's agreement. 개인연금/퇴직연금 are extra retirement products you choose yourself.
mistakes: Mixing up 연금 (pension) and 연봉 (annual salary) — they look similar but mean very different things.
Using 연금 for any monthly payment; it specifically means retirement income, not a subscription or installment.

usage: 오르다 is the default verb; 물가가 올랐어요 is everyday small talk
the cost of living is high
Koreans say 물가가 비싸다, treating overall prices as a thing that can be expensive
상승 = a rise; you'll see 물가 상승률 (inflation rate) in the news
안정되다 = to become stable; the opposite of runaway inflation
examples: 요즘 물가가 너무 올라서 장 보기 무서워요.
Prices have gone up so much lately that I'm scared to go grocery shopping.
장 보다 = to do grocery shopping; very common complaint among young residents
서울은 물가가 비싸지만 살기 편해요.
Seoul is expensive but convenient to live in.
Typical way to describe a city's cost of living
월급은 그대로인데 물가만 올라요.
My salary stays the same but only prices keep rising.
그대로 = unchanged; a relatable money gripe
nuance: 물가 refers to the general price level of goods and services, not the price tag on one item (that's 가격 or 값). When friends complain about inflation, they say 물가가 올랐다 rather than naming specific prices. It is one of the most-used words in casual money conversations in Korea right now.
mistakes: Saying 이 물가가 비싸요 about a single product — use 가격/값 for one item, 물가 only for overall prices.
Writing 물까 or 물카 — it is 물가, and the 가 is pronounced tense (mulkka) but still spelled 가.

usage: When 환율 rises, the won is weaker — bad for sending money home, good for incoming foreign cash
확인하다 — what you do before remitting or exchanging cash
좋다 here means favorable for you specifically
Phrase you'll type into a search before sending money abroad
examples: 오늘 환율이 좋아서 본국으로 송금했어요.
The rate was good today so I sent money back home.
Very practical for foreign residents; 송금 = remittance
환율 때문에 해외 직구가 비싸졌어요.
Overseas online shopping got expensive because of the exchange rate.
해외 직구 = direct overseas purchase, hugely popular in Korea
달러 환율이 1,400원을 넘었어요.
The dollar exchange rate passed 1,400 won.
Numbers like this come up constantly in 2020s Korea
nuance: 환율 is the rate between the won and a foreign currency, central to anyone who sends money abroad or shops on overseas sites. Saying 환율이 올랐다 means the foreign currency got more expensive in won, so it costs you more to buy dollars. Apps like Wise or your bank's 환율 우대 (rate discount) come up a lot.
mistakes: Confusing 환율 (exchange rate) with 환전 (the act of exchanging cash) — you 환전하다 at a rate, the rate itself is 환율.
Assuming 환율이 올랐다 is always good; for sending money home a higher won-per-dollar rate means you pay more.

usage: 붙다 (to stick) is the natural verb — your savings earn 이자가 붙어요
내다 when you owe it, e.g. on a loan (대출 이자)
율 = rate; also 금리 in formal/news contexts
높다/낮다 describe how much; high is great for savings, painful for loans
examples: 이 적금은 이자가 높은 편이에요.
This installment savings account has relatively high interest.
적금 = installment savings; -은 편이다 = relatively/on the higher side
대출 이자가 매달 나가서 부담돼요.
The loan interest goes out every month and it's a burden.
부담되다 = to feel like a financial burden, very common
요즘 금리가 올라서 이자가 늘었어요.
Rates went up lately so the interest increased.
Distinguishes 금리 (the rate) from 이자 (the actual money)
nuance: 이자 is the actual money — what your savings earn or what you owe on a loan. The rate itself is 이자율 or, more formally, 금리. Whether 이자 is good or bad depends entirely on which side you're on: 예금 이자 (deposit interest) is welcome, 대출 이자 (loan interest) hurts.
mistakes: Using 이자 for the rate — the percentage is 이자율/금리; 이자 is the won amount.
Saying 이자를 받다 about a loan you owe — you 내다 (pay) loan interest; you 받다 (receive) interest only on your own deposits.

usage: 갚다 = to pay back a debt; loan repayment is 원금 + 이자
보장 = guarantee; a key phrase when choosing safe vs. risky products
손실 = loss; the risk warning on funds and stocks
The two parts of any loan or deposit payout
examples: 이 상품은 원금이 보장돼요.
This product guarantees your principal.
보장되다 = to be guaranteed; reassuring for cautious savers
주식은 원금 손실 위험이 있어요.
Stocks carry the risk of losing your principal.
위험 = risk; standard disclaimer young investors hear
매달 원금이랑 이자를 같이 갚고 있어요.
I'm paying back the principal and interest together every month.
원금이랑 이자 = principal and interest, casual -이랑 connector
nuance: 원금 is the original sum you put in or borrowed, separate from the 이자 (interest) on top. 원금 보장 (principal protected) vs. 원금 손실 가능 (principal may be lost) is the single most important distinction when a bank or app offers you an investment. Watch for it whenever 펀드 or 주식 are involved.
mistakes: Confusing 원금 (principal) with 현금 (cash) — they sound a bit alike but are unrelated.
Thinking 원금 보장 means profit is guaranteed; it only means you won't lose your initial amount, not that you'll gain.

usage: to sign up for a fund
가입하다 — the verb for buying into a fund at a bank/app
투자하다 = to invest; the general action
수익률 = rate of return; what you check to see if you're up or down
적립식 = paying in a fixed amount each month, popular for beginners
examples: 은행에서 펀드를 추천받았는데 좀 고민돼요.
The bank recommended a fund but I'm a bit torn.
추천받다 = to get recommended; 고민되다 = to feel torn/unsure
저는 매달 조금씩 펀드에 넣고 있어요.
I put a little into a fund each month.
넣다 (to put in) is the everyday verb for contributing money
펀드는 원금을 잃을 수도 있어요.
With a fund you could lose your principal.
Important risk reminder linking back to 원금
nuance: 펀드 is a pooled investment product (mutual fund) you usually buy through a bank app or securities account. Unlike a 예금/적금, a 펀드 has no guaranteed return and your 원금 is at risk. Many 20-30s start with an 적립식 펀드 or jump to 주식/ETF on apps like 토스증권 or 키움.
mistakes: Spelling it 펀트 — it is 펀드, from English 'fund'.
Assuming a 펀드 works like a savings account; it is not 원금 보장, so returns can be negative.

usage: 쓰다 (to write) is the set verb — 가계부 쓰다 = to track spending
Most people now use a 가계부 앱 like 뱅크샐러드 instead of paper
to tidy up / review the budget
정리하다 = to organize, e.g. at month's end
to write down in the budget
적다 = to jot down each expense
examples: 이번 달부터 가계부를 쓰기 시작했어요.
I started keeping a budget this month.
Common New-Year/new-month resolution
가계부를 보니까 배달 음식에 돈을 너무 많이 썼어요.
Looking at my budget, I spent way too much on delivery food.
Very relatable for young Koreans; 배달 음식 = delivery food
저는 가계부 앱으로 카드 내역을 자동으로 관리해요.
I manage my card history automatically with a budgeting app.
내역 = transaction history; apps auto-import it
nuance: 가계부 literally means household-account book, but today it almost always refers to a budgeting app that auto-syncs your cards and accounts. Writing one (가계부 쓰다) is a classic money-saving habit, especially when people realize how much goes to 배달 and 카페. It pairs naturally with 지출 and 절약.
mistakes: Saying 가계부를 만들다 for daily tracking — the habitual verb is 가계부를 쓰다.
Confusing 가계부 (your personal budget) with 영수증 (receipt) or 명세서 (statement) — those are inputs to the 가계부.

usage: to build up an emergency fund
모으다 = to gather/save up over time
to dip into the emergency fund
쓰다 when an emergency finally forces you to use it
숨기다 = to hide; jokingly, money hidden from a partner
A separate 통장 (account) people keep just for emergencies
examples: 갑자기 병원비가 나와서 비상금을 썼어요.
I had a sudden hospital bill so I used my emergency fund.
병원비 = medical costs; classic emergency-fund use
매달 조금씩 비상금을 모으고 있어요.
I'm saving up a little emergency money each month.
조금씩 = little by little, the realistic approach
비상금은 따로 통장에 넣어 두세요.
Keep your emergency fund in a separate account.
따로 = separately; -어 두다 = do in advance and keep that way
nuance: 비상금 is money set aside for emergencies — sudden medical bills, job loss, a broken phone. It carries a slightly playful second meaning too: secret stash money hidden from a spouse or partner, which shows up in dramas and memes. Financial-advice content for 20-30s constantly recommends building a 비상금 first.
mistakes: Confusing 비상금 (emergency savings) with 용돈 (allowance/pocket money) — 용돈 is for everyday spending, 비상금 is untouched until an emergency.
Treating 비상금 as investment money; the point is that it stays safe and instantly accessible, not that it grows.

usage: 늘다/줄다 for income going up or down
세 = tax; the tax levied on your 소득
증명 = proof; 소득 증명서 is needed for visas, loans, leases
고정 = fixed; a regular salary vs. irregular freelance income
examples: 대출을 받으려면 소득 증명이 필요해요.
You need proof of income to take out a loan.
Very practical; also required for some visa renewals
부업으로 소득을 조금 늘렸어요.
I increased my income a bit with a side job.
부업 = side job; the side-hustle trend is big among 20-30s
소득이 일정하지 않아서 저축이 어려워요.
My income isn't steady so saving is hard.
일정하다 = to be regular/consistent; the freelancer's struggle
nuance: 소득 is the formal word for income or earnings, used in official contexts — taxes (소득세), loan and visa paperwork (소득 증명), and statistics. In casual chat about your paycheck people often just say 월급, but the moment documents or taxes are involved it becomes 소득. It's the natural counterpart to 지출.
mistakes: Using 소득 only for salary — it covers all earnings including freelance, rental, and investment income.
Confusing 소득 (income you earn) with 수익 (profit/return from an investment); they overlap but 수익 implies a gain on something invested.

usage: 줄이다 = to reduce; the core money-saving move
고정 = fixed; rent, 관리비, subscriptions that recur each month
많다/적다 to describe how much you spend
내역 = itemized record, what a 가계부 app shows you
examples: 이번 달은 지출이 너무 많았어요.
I spent way too much this month.
Typical end-of-month reflection
고정 지출부터 줄여 보세요.
Try cutting your fixed expenses first.
Standard budgeting advice; -어 보다 = give it a try
수입과 지출을 비교해 봤어요.
I compared my income and spending.
수입과 지출 (income and spending) is a very common pairing
nuance: 지출 means money going out — your spending or expenses — and is the natural opposite of 소득/수입. Budgeting talk constantly contrasts 수입 vs 지출, and the first advice is always 고정 지출 (fixed costs) 줄이기. It feels a touch more formal than just 돈 쓰다 but is completely normal in everyday money conversations.
mistakes: Confusing 지출 (money going out) with 지급 (a payment being made/disbursed) — they look similar but 지급 is about issuing payment, often from an institution.
Pairing it as 소득과 지출 only; the very common everyday pairing is 수입과 지출.

usage: Add 하다 to make it a verb; 전기를 절약하다 = save electricity
Also seen on appliances and public-campaign signs
정신 = spirit/mindset; praising someone's frugal habits
절약 isn't only money — 시간 절약 = time-saving
examples: 요즘 돈을 아끼려고 외식을 줄이고 절약하고 있어요.
Lately I'm cutting eating out and economizing to save money.
아끼다 = to use sparingly; pairs naturally with 절약
전기를 절약하면 관리비가 줄어요.
If you save electricity, your maintenance fee goes down.
관리비 = building maintenance fee, a real monthly cost
대중교통을 이용하면 교통비를 절약할 수 있어요.
Using public transport lets you save on transport costs.
교통비 = transport expenses; classic 절약 example
nuance: 절약 is the noun for thrift or economizing, turned into a verb with 하다 (절약하다). It applies to money, energy, and time alike, and carries a positive, virtuous tone — being good at 절약 is a compliment. It often appears alongside 아끼다 (to use sparingly) and is the goal behind keeping a 가계부.
mistakes: Confusing 절약 (deliberate, sensible saving) with 저축 (putting money into savings) — 절약 is spending less, 저축 is stashing money away.
Using 절약 to mean stingy in a negative way; that's 인색하다 or 짠돌이 — 절약 itself is positive.
